entities.summary:
The State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, known from 1992 to 2003 as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (FRY), represented the final, transitional iteration of the Yugoslav state, existing from April 27, 1992, until June 3, 2006. Located in the heart of the Balkans in Southeast Europe, this polity emerged from the violent dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and ultimately dissolved into two independent sovereign states. Its existence was characterized by complex internal political dynamics, international isolation, and a persistent struggle to define its identity and territorial integrity in the post-Cold War European landscape, making it a critical case study in state secession and regional geopolitics.

Initially comprising the Republic of Serbia (including its autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo) and the Republic of Montenegro, the FRY was formed after four of the six constituent republics of the SFRY declared independence. Under the leadership of figures like Slobodan Milošević, the FRY was deeply implicated in the Yugoslav Wars of the 1990s, particularly the Bosnian War and the Kosovo War, leading to severe international sanctions and the NATO bombing campaign in 1999. In February 2003, under pressure from the European Union and seeking to normalize its international standing, the FRY formally transformed into the looser State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, adopting a new constitutional charter that granted greater autonomy to its two constituent republics and included a provision for future independence referendums.
